Cornell University's main campus in Ithaca is located in the [Finger Lakes](/wiki/Finger_Lakes "Finger Lakes") region in [upstate New York](/wiki/Upstate_New_York "Upstate New York") and features views of the [city](/wiki/Ithaca,_New_York "Ithaca, New York"), [Cayuga Lake](/wiki/Cayuga_Lake "Cayuga Lake"), and surrounding valleys. The campus is bordered by two [gorges](/wiki/Gorge "Gorge"), Fall Creek Gorge and Cascadilla Gorge. The gorges are popular swimming spots during warmer months, but their use is discouraged by the university and city code due to potential safety hazards.[[57]](#cite_note-58) Adjacent to the main campus, Cornell owns the 2,800 acres (1,100 ha) [Cornell Botanic Gardens](/wiki/Cornell_Botanic_Gardens "Cornell Botanic Gardens"), which feature cultivated gardens, arboretum collections, and natural areas.[[58]](#cite_note-59)

Elected mayor of Philadelphia in 1991, he inherited a $250 million deficit and the lowest credit rating of any major city in the country. As mayor, he balanced Philadelphia's budget and generated a budget surplus while cutting business and wage taxes and dramatically improving services to Philadelphia neighborhoods. *[The New York Times](/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")* stated that Philadelphia under Rendell "has made one of the most stunning turnarounds in recent urban history."[[2]](#cite_note-2) Nicknamed "America's Mayor" by [Al Gore](/wiki/Al_Gore "Al Gore"),[[3]](#cite_note-3) Rendell served as chairman of the [Democratic National Committee](/wiki/Democratic_National_Committee "Democratic National Committee") during the [2000 presidential election](/wiki/2000_United_States_presidential_election "2000 United States presidential election").

In [2002](/wiki/2002_Pennsylvania_gubernatorial_election "2002 Pennsylvania gubernatorial election"), Rendell was elected governor of [Pennsylvania](/wiki/Pennsylvania "Pennsylvania"). He was a member of the [Democratic Governors Association](/wiki/Democratic_Governors_Association "Democratic Governors Association") Executive Committee and served as the chairman of the [National Governors Association](/wiki/National_Governors_Association "National Governors Association"). He was reelected in a landslide in [2006](/wiki/2006_Pennsylvania_gubernatorial_election "2006 Pennsylvania gubernatorial election"). He left office in 2011 due to term limits, and released a book, *A Nation of Wusses: How America's Leaders Lost the Guts to Make Us Great*, the following year. In early 1992 it was confirmed that Soviet forces in Cuba had already received tactical nuclear warheads for their [artillery rockets](/wiki/Rocket_artillery "Rocket artillery") and [Il-28 bombers](/wiki/Ilyushin_Il-28 "Ilyushin Il-28") when the crisis broke.[[221]](#cite_note-aca-224) Castro stated that he would have recommended their use if the US had invaded, even if Cuba was destroyed.[[221]](#cite_note-aca-224)

Fifty years after the crisis, [Graham Allison](/wiki/Graham_Allison "Graham Allison") wrote:

> Fifty years ago, the Cuban Missile Crisis brought the world to the brink of nuclear disaster. During the standoff, US President John F. Kennedy thought the chance of escalation to war was "between 1 in 3 and even", and what we have learned in later decades has done nothing to lengthen those odds. We now know, for example, that in addition to nuclear-armed ballistic missiles, the Soviet Union had deployed 100 tactical nuclear weapons to Cuba, and the local Soviet commander there could have launched these weapons without additional codes or commands from Moscow. The US air strike and invasion that were scheduled for the third week of the confrontation would likely have triggered a nuclear response against American ships and troops, and perhaps even [Miami](/wiki/Miami "Miami"). The resulting war might have led to the deaths of over 100 million Americans and over 100 million Russians.[[222]](#cite_note-225)[[223]](#cite_note-226)

[BBC](/wiki/BBC "BBC") journalist Joe Matthews published the story, on 13 October 2012, after news of the 100 tactical nuclear warheads mentioned by Graham Allison in the excerpt above.[[224]](#cite_note-MatthewsBBC20121013-227) Khrushchev feared that Castro's hurt pride and widespread Cuban indignation over the concessions he had made to Kennedy might lead to a breakdown of the agreement between the Soviet Union and the United States. *Funeral* and the single "[Cold Wind](/wiki/Cold_Wind "Cold Wind")" were nominated for [Grammys](/wiki/Grammy "Grammy") in the [Best Alternative Rock Album](/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Alternative_Music_Album "Grammy Award for Best Alternative Music Album") and [Best Song Written for a Motion Picture, Television or Other Visual Media](/wiki/Grammy_Award_for_Best_Song_Written_for_a_Motion_Picture,_Television_or_Other_Visual_Media "Grammy Award for Best Song Written for a Motion Picture, Television or Other Visual Media") categories (*Six Feet Under, Vol. 2: Everything Ends*), respectively. On April 2, 2006, in [Halifax, Nova Scotia](/wiki/Halifax_Urban_Area "Halifax Urban Area"), Arcade Fire received the [Juno Award](/wiki/Juno_Award "Juno Award") for Songwriters Of The Year for three songs from *Funeral*: "Wake Up", "Rebellion (Lies)", and "Neighborhood #3 (Power Out)".[[30]](#cite_note-30) The band was nominated for three [BRIT Awards](/wiki/BRIT_Awards "BRIT Awards"): Best International Group, Best International Album, and Best International Breakthrough Act.[[31]](#cite_note-31)

Arcade Fire made an appearance on the BBC show *[Later with Jools Holland](/wiki/Later_with_Jools_Holland "Later with Jools Holland")* on May 12, 2005, performing "Power Out" and "Rebellion (Lies)". On October 22, 2007, *Funeral* was ranked No.8 in [Bob Mersereau](/wiki/Bob_Mersereau "Bob Mersereau")'s book *[The Top 100 Canadian Albums](/wiki/The_Top_100_Canadian_Albums "The Top 100 Canadian Albums")*.[[32]](#cite_note-32) In late 2009, Pitchfork ranked the album No.2 in their list of the top 200 albums of the 2000s, behind [Radiohead](/wiki/Radiohead "Radiohead")'s *[Kid A](/wiki/Kid_A "Kid A")*.[[33]](#cite_note-33)

The percentage of the population at risk of [relative poverty](/wiki/Relative_poverty "Relative poverty") was 21% in 2004 – one of the highest rates in the European Union.[[226]](#cite_note-226) Ireland's inequality of income distribution score on the [Gini coefficient](/wiki/Gini_coefficient "Gini coefficient") scale was 30.4 in 2000, slightly below the OECD average of 31.[[227]](#cite_note-227) The daily [median income](/wiki/Median_income "Median income") was $50.49 ([PPP](/wiki/Purchasing_power_parity "Purchasing power parity")) in 2023.[[228]](#cite_note-r236-228) Sustained increases in the value of residential property during the 1990s and up to late 2006 was a key factor in the increase in personal wealth in Ireland, with Ireland ranking second only to Japan in personal wealth in 2006.[[229]](#cite_note-229)

From 1975 to 2005, tax revenues fluctuated at around 30% of GDP (see graph right).

Fairly solid evidence indicates that coast redwoods were the world's largest trees before logging, with numerous historical specimens reportedly over 122 m (400 ft).[[77]](#cite_note-vanpelt-77): 16, 42 The theoretical maximum potential height of coast redwoods is thought to be limited to between 122 and 130 m (400 and 427 ft), as [evapotranspiration](/wiki/Evapotranspiration "Evapotranspiration") is insufficient to transport water to leaves beyond this range.[[46]](#cite_note-Koch2004-46) Further studies have indicated that this maximum requires fog, which is prevalent in these trees' natural environment.[[78]](#cite_note-78)

A tree reportedly 114.3 m (375 ft) in length was felled in Sonoma County by the Murphy Brothers saw mill in the 1870s,[[79]](#cite_note-79) another claimed to be 115.8 m (380 ft) and 7.9 m (26 ft) in diameter was cut down near Eureka in 1914,[[80]](#cite_note-Carder-80)[[81]](#cite_note-81) and the [Lindsay Creek Tree](/wiki/Lindsay_Creek_Tree "Lindsay Creek Tree") was documented to have a height of 120 m (390 ft) when it was uprooted and felled by a storm in 1905. fanoutqa_029989.x:
Lonzo Ball :: Professional career :: Los Angeles Lakers (2017–2019) :: 2017–18 season: Rookie season :: part 01 :: chunk_0005
[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/31/Lonzo_Ball_smile_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Lonzo_Ball_smile_%28cropped%29.jpg)](/wiki/File:Lonzo_Ball_smile_(cropped).jpg)

Ball in 2018

Ball was selected with the second overall pick of the [2017 NBA draft](/wiki/2017_NBA_draft "2017 NBA draft") by his hometown team the [Los Angeles Lakers](/wiki/Los_Angeles_Lakers "Los Angeles Lakers").[[53]](#cite_note-53) It was the third straight year they had the No. 2 pick.[[54]](#cite_note-54) He and [Brandon Ingram](/wiki/Brandon_Ingram "Brandon Ingram"), their second overall pick from the previous year, headlined a young core for the Lakers.[[55]](#cite_note-55) [D'Angelo Russell](/wiki/D%27Angelo_Russell "D'Angelo Russell"), their No. 2 pick in 2015, was traded days earlier, partly to clear the way for their newly drafted point guard. Lakers president of basketball operations [Magic Johnson](/wiki/Magic_Johnson "Magic Johnson") billed Ball as "the new face of the Lakers."[[56]](#cite_note-56) During the [2017 NBA Summer League](/wiki/2017_NBA_Summer_League "2017 NBA Summer League") in [Las Vegas](/wiki/Las_Vegas "Las Vegas"), Ball was named the league MVP after averaging 16.3 points, 9.3 assists, 7.7 rebounds, 2.5 steals, and 1.0 blocks per game. He had two triple-doubles, the first in Vegas since 2008 and the first ever in Vegas by a rookie.[[57]](#cite_note-57)[[58]](#cite_note-58) He had four games with 10 or more assists, becoming the first in league history to have more than 10 assists in more than one game; his 9.3 assist average was also a league record.[[59]](#cite_note-59)[[60]](#cite_note-60)
